title: How to block pop-ups in Safari on Mac: per-site and all-website settings explained
metaTitle: How to Block Pop-ups in Safari on Mac, Step by Step
description: How to block pop-ups in Safari on Mac: open Safari > Settings, click Websites, then set Pop-up Windows for each site or all sites.
targetKeyword: how to block pop-ups in safari on mac
secondaryKeywords: allow pop-ups for one site Safari
intro: To block pop-ups in Safari on Mac, choose Safari > Settings, click Websites, then click Pop-up Windows in the left sidebar. Set a rule for one site under Configured Websites, or use the When visiting other websites menu to set the default for every site.
tldr: Open Safari > Settings, click Websites, then click Pop-up Windows in the left sidebar.
Use a site's pop-up menu to choose Allow, Block and Notify, or Block for that site only.
Remove conflicting entries under Configured Websites before you change the default for all websites.
Block and Notify hides pop-ups, but the Show button in the Smart Search field can display them later.
If pop-ups still appear on a blocked site, check Configured Websites, the Extensions tab, and the Applications folder.

blocks.text: Safari keeps its pop-up controls in one place. The same window that sets a rule for one website also sets the default for every other site. Once you know the path, you can change it in a few minutes. This page covers the three choices, the rule that makes conflicting entries matter, and what to do when pop-ups keep showing up anyway.
Where the pop-up setting lives

Apple's guide gives one path. You open Safari's Settings window, go to Websites, and pick Pop-up Windows from the left sidebar. The sidebar can run long, so if you can't see the item, scroll to the bottom of the list.

Apple's current pages say Safari > Settings. Some search results and older guides say Preferences. If your menu says Preferences, compare the labels on your screen with the ones here before you click. Apple's Safari 18.0 guide, written for macOS 15 Sequoia, uses the same labels as the current page.
The three choices, and what each one does
Every pop-up rule uses one of three choices. The pop-up menu beside a site and the menu for all other websites offer the same three. The table shows what each one does and when it makes sense.

rows: A site uses a pop-up for something you need, such as a login or a payment window.
Pop-ups stay hidden. You can display them with the Show button in the Smart Search field.
You want quiet pages, but you might need a blocked window later.
Pop-ups stay hidden, with no notification.
You never want to see them, and you don't need to recover one.
blocks.caption: The three choices in the Pop-up Windows setting, as Apple describes them.

blocks.text: Block and Notify is the choice most people miss. Blocked pop-ups stay hidden, but the Show button lets you display them. Apple describes that button only by its icon, so look for the icon, not a text label. With Block, there is no notice and no button to find.
Block pop-ups on one website only

A per-site rule beats the default. That makes it the right tool when most sites should stay quiet but one site needs its window. A bank site that opens a statement in a new window is one example. You can set that one site to Allow and leave the default alone.

Sites with a rule appear under Configured Websites. To change a rule, select the site, click Remove, then set the option you want. Apple's wording makes this two moves: remove the old rule, then set the new one. Doing it in that order keeps the list clean.

Here is a worked example. A news site opens a subscription window every time you load an article. Find that site under Configured Websites, set it to Block, and leave the default as it is. Every other site keeps the rule you chose for it.
Set the default for all other websites
The default applies to every site that has no rule of its own. It sits under the label When visiting other websites. Choose Allow, Block and Notify, or Block from that menu.

Order matters here. Apple says to remove conflicting entries under Configured Websites before you set the default. A site with its own Allow entry ignores the default, so a leftover entry keeps its pop-ups running. Clean the list first, change the default, then test.

Block and Notify is a practical default for most people. It stops pop-ups from opening, and the Show button gives you a way back to a window that a page actually needs. Allow only the few sites that need pop-ups for real work.
Why a site still shows pop-ups after you block it
If you set a site to Block and pop-ups still appear, something else is opening them. Apple gives three checks. Work through them in order, starting with the one you control.

items: Check Configured Websites for the site. Look for an Allow entry you forgot about, since it overrides the setting you chose.
Open Safari > Settings > Extensions and review what is installed. Turn off or remove any extension you don't recognize.
Open the Applications folder in Finder and look for apps you don't remember installing. Apple says unwanted software may cause pop-ups on a blocked site.

blocks.text: Go slowly with the third check. Remove only apps you can identify and trust. Deleting the wrong app can break something you use every day. If you're unsure about an app, search its name first.
Fake close buttons and pop-ups you can't escape
Some pop-up pages draw a fake close button. Clicking it can open another page or start a download. Apple advises closing the whole window or tab instead.
If a page traps you, use the Search field to go somewhere else. Apple suggests this before you try anything more involved.

Pop-ups can come back the next time Safari opens, because Safari may restore the windows you had open. Quit Safari, then hold Shift while you reopen it. Holding Shift skips restoring windows. Apple names Shift as the only key for this step, and it lists no shortcut for the settings themselves.
When blocking breaks a page you need

Apple warns that blocking pop-ups can also block content you want to see. Login windows, payment steps, and document viewers sometimes open in a new window. A blocked one can leave a page half loaded.
Fix it with a per-site Allow, not by changing the default. Keep the default on Block and Notify, then allow only the site that breaks. The rest of the web stays quiet.
Change one thing at a time. Set one site, reload the page, and see whether the content loads. If you change five settings at once, you won't know which one fixed or broke the page.
Pop-ups on iPhone and iPad
The iPhone and iPad path is different. Open Settings, tap Apps, tap Safari, then turn on the Block Pop-ups toggle. Apple calls this the iOS and iPadOS equivalent of the Mac steps.
The Mac gives you more control, because you can set rules site by site. The iPhone and iPad path in Apple's guide is a single toggle. If you use both devices, set your preference on each one.
How common ad blocking is

Ad blocking is common. eyeo, which makes an ad blocker, estimates that about 1.1 billion people ran ad blockers in Q4 2025. By its count, that is about 30% of internet users. eyeo counts people who took a deliberate step to install an ad-blocking product, so treat the figure as a vendor estimate, not an independent count.

Pop-up blocking and ad blocking are different controls. The pop-up setting handles pop-up windows. Ad blockers are separate tools that you add to Safari as extensions, and the Extensions tab in Safari's settings is where you review them.
Which Safari and macOS versions these steps cover

Apple's pop-up pages do not state a Safari or macOS version, so this page relies on what those pages show. The Safari 18.0 guide uses the same path and labels as the current guide. That is the strongest evidence available from Apple's pages.

The newest release is macOS 27 Golden Gate. According to 9to5Mac, its Safari changes are tab grouping by topic, Notify Me, Describe an Extension, and pull-to-refresh. None of those reports mention pop-up blocking.
If your Safari looks different, check the Apple guide for your version and compare labels. Trust what your screen shows over an older screenshot.
Mistakes people make with pop-up settings

items: Changing the default without removing old site rules. The old rule keeps its own setting, so the change seems to fail.
Choosing Allow for one site to fix a single window, then forgetting it. The rule stays until you remove it.
Clicking a fake close button. Close the window or tab instead.
Expecting Block to send a notice. Block hides pop-ups with no notification, so you may never know one was stopped.
Treating Shift as a blocking key. Apple uses Shift only when you reopen Safari to skip restoring windows.

blocks.text: What to do next
Start with the default. Set it to Block and Notify, then browse your usual sites for a while. Add a per-site Allow only when a page needs it.
Review Configured Websites now and then. Remove sites you no longer visit, since their rules still apply. If pop-ups return after all of this, check Applications and the Extensions tab again.

faq.question: Where is the pop-up setting in Safari on Mac?
faq.answer: Choose Safari > Settings, click Websites, then click Pop-up Windows in the left sidebar. If you don't see it, scroll to the bottom of the sidebar list.

faq.question: What is the difference between Block and Block and Notify?
faq.answer: Both hide pop-ups. Block and Notify lets you display blocked pop-ups later with the Show button in the Smart Search field. Block hides them with no notification, so there is nothing to show.

faq.question: How do I allow pop-ups on just one website?
faq.answer: Find the site under Configured Websites. Select it, click Remove, then set its option to Allow from its pop-up menu. Leave the default on Block so other sites stay blocked.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut for blocking pop-ups in Safari?
faq.answer: Apple's pop-up guide lists no keyboard shortcut for this task. The only key it mentions is Shift, which you hold while reopening Safari to skip restoring windows. Use the menu path for the settings.

faq.question: Why do pop-ups still appear after I block them?
faq.answer: Check Configured Websites for a leftover Allow entry first. Then review the Extensions tab and the Applications folder for software you don't recognize, which Apple says can be the cause.

faq.question: Does blocking pop-ups in Safari also block ads?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. The pop-up setting controls pop-up windows. Ad blockers are separate Safari extensions, so the two are different controls.

faq.question: Do these steps work on iPhone?
faq.answer: Not the same way. On iPhone and iPad, go to Settings > Apps > Safari and turn on the Block Pop-ups toggle. The Mac version offers per-site rules.

faq.question: Do these steps work on older versions of Safari?
faq.answer: Apple's pages do not give a version number for these steps. Apple's Safari 18.0 guide uses the same labels, but its pages do not confirm older releases, so compare labels on your screen if they differ.

steps.name: Open Safari Settings
steps.text: Click Safari in the menu bar at the top of the screen, then click Settings. Apple's current guide uses this label. If your menu says Preferences, click that item instead.
steps.tip: Make sure Safari is the active app. Its name appears in the menu bar next to the Apple logo.

steps.name: Open the Websites section
steps.text: In the Settings window, click Websites. This section holds the rules for each site, plus the default for every other site.
steps.tip: If the window looks cramped, make it larger by dragging a corner.

steps.name: Choose Pop-up Windows
steps.text: In the left sidebar, click Pop-up Windows. If you don't see it, scroll to the bottom of the sidebar list.
steps.tip: Check the label before you click, because the sidebar holds other entries too.

steps.name: Set a rule for one site (optional)
steps.text: Select the site under Configured Websites, click Remove, then set the option you want for that site from its pop-up menu. Skip this step if you only want a default.
steps.tip: A site rule overrides the default, so it stays in effect even after you change the default.

steps.name: Clear conflicting entries, then set the default
steps.text: Remove any Configured Websites entry that conflicts with the default you want. Then open the When visiting other websites menu and choose Allow, Block and Notify, or Block.
steps.tip: Block and Notify keeps the Show button available, so you can recover a hidden window.

steps.name: Test the change
steps.text: Close the Settings window and visit a site that uses pop-ups. If Block and Notify hid one, look for the Show button in the Smart Search field and click it to display the window.
steps.tip: Apple describes the Show button only by its icon, so look for the icon rather than a text label.

troubleshooting.problem: Pop-ups still show on a site I blocked
troubleshooting.fix: Open Configured Websites and look for a leftover Allow entry. Remove it and set the rule again. If pop-ups continue, check the Extensions tab and the Applications folder.

troubleshooting.problem: A login or payment window won't open
troubleshooting.fix: Set only that site to Allow. Keep the default on Block and Notify, then reload the page.

troubleshooting.problem: Blocked pop-ups don't show up anywhere
troubleshooting.fix: Check your default. Only Block and Notify gives you the Show button in the Smart Search field. With Block, blocked pop-ups are hidden with no notice.

troubleshooting.problem: A fake close button opens another page
troubleshooting.fix: Don't click it. Close the window or tab instead. If the page traps you, use the Search field to go somewhere else.
Quit Safari, then hold Shift while you reopen it. Holding Shift skips restoring windows from the last session.
